content.intro: In this lesson, you will study game-Playing and Adversarial Search within Traditional AI, Logic, Search, and Reasoning. You will connect the syllabus topics below to a small, inspectable example and practice stating what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: Traditional AI represents states, facts, goals, and actions explicitly. A search or rule-based method is only as useful as its representation and assumptions.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: Adversarial search evaluates action sequences when another decision-maker also tries to optimize an outcome. Minimax models opposing objectives, while alpha–beta pruning can skip branches without changing the result under the same assumptions.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus topics covered in this lesson

items.title: Game trees
items.text: Game trees is one of the concepts used to reason about game-playing and adversarial search. Define the inputs, assumptions, and intended result in this context, then test the idea on a small representative example and document where it may not apply.

items.title: Minimax algorithm
items.text: Minimax considers how an opponent might respond and selects an action by backing values up through a game tree. The result depends on the search depth and the quality of the leaf evaluation function.

items.title: Alpha-beta pruning
items.text: Alpha–beta pruning skips branches that cannot change the minimax decision. It improves search efficiency when applied correctly without changing the result under the same evaluation and search assumptions.

content_blocks.text: If the output differs, check indentation and spelling, confirm you saved the intended file, and compare each input value with the example.
